solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Chop off round extremely silly hair-raising feature

indicators.note: one set of letters goes round the other, enclosing it
something that has gone off is spoiled or out of order, so the word before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: taking a word to its extremes keeps only its two end letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of silly

explanation.surface: A barber is told to lop off a ridiculous, frightening hairstyle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hair-raising' tempts you towards barbering; here it means terrifying, and the feature is a film, Hitchcock's PSYCHO.
explanation.definitionFit: A feature is a full-length film, and Hitchcock's Psycho is the classic scary one.

clue.text: Not buying plastic surgery, church being involved

indicators.note: something involved is drawn inside, so these letters sit within the others
surgery reshapes a body, so the letters of the word before it are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone is unconvinced by cosmetic surgery, especially with the church getting mixed up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic surgery' reads as one phrase, but plastic is the raw material and surgery the signal to rework it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'I'm not buying it' is an idiom for disbelief, so someone not buying a claim is doubtful of it.

clue.text: Sound when Cyclops is stuffing a cult hero

indicators.note: stuffing goes inside something, so these letters are packed into the hero's name

parts.note: Che Guevara, the revolutionary on a million T-shirts
the setter speaking of himself: I
with I, 'Cyclops is' becomes I'M

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of making noise while cramming a hero-worshipped figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by their pseudonym, so 'Cyclops is' stands for I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: A chime is a ringing bell-like sound, and to chime is to make one.

clue.text: Love tips from Wills and Kate holding newly-delivered George (not the popular one)

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so the next part sits inside

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

indicators.note: the tips of words are their ends, and here the final letters are taken

parts.note: last letter of Wills
a newly delivered baby has just been born
last letter of Kate

explanation.surface: Fond greetings to William and Catherine with their new son, Prince George, and a dig at another George.
explanation.walkthrough: Written when Prince George was born in 2013; the other, unpopular George is George Osborne, then the Chancellor running austerity.
explanation.definitionFit: George Osborne was the much-disliked Chancellor of the Exchequer, unlike the popular new prince of the same name.

clue.text: Peter out to crush Adele's debut shit Brit blast

indicators.note: crushing something squeezes it inside, so the other letters are pressed in

parts.note: to peter out is to fade away, to die

indicators.note: something shit is a mess, so the letters next to it are muddled
a debut is a first appearance, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: first letter of Adele
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A rant: someone called Peter is out to crush the singer Adele's first record as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' looks like a name but 'Peter out' is a verb meaning fade or die.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a furious verbal attack, and a blast is a burst of angry criticism.

clue.text: Balls up and allow drug to take out?

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the letters from the bottom

parts.note: Ed Balls, the Labour politician, gives his first name
to allow is to let
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: A mess-up: permitting a drug to be removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls up' looks like a cock-up, but Balls is Ed Balls, a Labour shadow minister at the time.
explanation.definitionFit: To delete something is to remove or strike it out, as with text.

clue.text: Bastard not available on left side

parts.note: an arse is an obnoxious person
NA is the standard abbreviation for not available
L for left

explanation.surface: A rotter who is unavailable is grumbled about on the left wing of a team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side' looks like part of 'left side' but is the definition; ARSE is British slang for a contemptible person.
explanation.definitionFit: A side is a sports team, and Arsenal is the London football club.

clue.text: "Hitler, loon, has only got one ball", working as an angry parting shot?

indicators.note: working things are being processed, so the remaining letters are reworked
a ball is round like the letter O, so having only one means one of a pair of those letters is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, minus one round letter

explanation.surface: The wartime song's jibe about Hitler, flung as a furious farewell.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface quotes the British wartime song 'Hitler has only got one ball'; the line is also the deletion instruction, removing one of the two Os in loon.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Rot in hell!' is a vicious curse said to someone you are leaving behind for good.

clue.text: see 17ac.
Broadcast gaffes badly aimed by Shadow minister

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Ed Balls was Labour's shadow Chancellor

explanation.surface: An opposition politician's poorly targeted blunders on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls, Labour's shadow Chancellor, was famous for awkward interviews, so his surname is apt for media slip-ups.
explanation.definitionFit: Balls-ups are blunders, so media balls are slip-ups made in front of the press or cameras.

clue.text: see 26ac.
Balls, say, on decline?

indicators.note: in an across entry, one word sitting on another means it comes first in the line

parts.note: to say is to utter
to decline is to rot or decay

explanation.surface: A question about whether Balls is, so to speak, going downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: Balls has been Ed Balls elsewhere in this puzzle; here it means nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Balls is British slang for nonsense, and utter rot is complete rubbish.

clue.text: Neglected state of one rogue taking tabloid over

indicators.note: turned over means flipped back to front
to take something in is to hold it inside
a rogue misbehaves, so the letters of the word before it run out of order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: A neglected state is blamed on a scoundrel taking over a tabloid newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at a press baron buying a paper; the Sun is the British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonuse is the condition of not being used, a state of neglect.

clue.text: Bitchy type's after 'Pinnacle of Sadism' belt

indicators.note: one part comes after another, so it is placed second
a pinnacle is the top, the first letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the first letter of Sadism
a carper is a nagging fault-finder

explanation.surface: A catty person's remark follows the peak of cruelty, a lashing with a belt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belt' looks like a strap to hit with; here it is a verb meaning to run off fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To belt is to go at full speed, and to scarper is British slang for running away quickly.

clue.text: Reduced the invading viral, yet crap schedules filler

indicators.note: an invader goes inside, so this letter sits within the rest
something crap is a mess, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: a word reduced to almost nothing keeps just its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the

explanation.surface: A grumble that a cheap, hyped show is invading the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's opinion of the genre is built in: 'crap' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Reality television is cheap programming used to fill broadcasters' schedules.

clue.text: President wasted, being carried by crestfallen Democrats

definitions.note: Allende died in the 1973 Chilean coup

indicators.note: something carried is held inside, so the letters are tucked within the following words

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A defeated president is propped up by downcast members of his party.
explanation.walkthrough: Salvador Allende, Chile's socialist president, died when Pinochet's coup overthrew him in 1973.
explanation.definitionFit: Allende was the Chilean president killed in the 1973 military coup, so he is a president who was wiped out.

clue.text: Merkel's article: "Reform, I urge you ultimately!" must be done

parts.note: DER is a German definite article, Angela Merkel being German

indicators.note: to reform something is to shape it anew, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of you

explanation.surface: Angela Merkel writes a piece urging reform as essential.
explanation.walkthrough: The German chancellor's 'article' is grammatical, not a newspaper piece.
explanation.definitionFit: De rigueur, borrowed from French, describes what etiquette or fashion requires, something obligatory.

clue.text: (& 8dn.) Absolute crap, many society events

parts.note: a load of means lots of
balls are formal dances in high society

explanation.surface: A sneer that the social season's many dances are worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: Balls has appeared as Ed Balls and as nonsense in this puzzle; here it is a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: 'A load of balls' is British slang for total nonsense or rubbish.

clue.text: Sixty Seconds Erection Point: American special edition

indicators.note: an erection rises, and in a down entry rising means read from the bottom up

parts.note: a mo is a moment, roughly a minute
a nib is the point of a pen
US for American

explanation.surface: It reads like a lurid tabloid headline about a sixty-second erection, sold as a special issue.
explanation.walkthrough: MO is British slang for a moment, as in 'half a mo'.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnibus is a volume or broadcast collecting several works or episodes, a special compilation edition.

clue.text: High flier responsible for the blue joke

parts.note: the blue is the sky
a lark is a prank or bit of fun

explanation.surface: A highly placed person is behind a dirty joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue joke' reads as a rude joke; the blue is the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The skylark is a songbird famous for singing while hovering very high above fields.

clue.text: "F—k!" (as H. Mirren plays host to a region)

indicators.note: a host contains the guest, so the letters are found inside the preceding words

parts.note: runs from the end of the swear word into the actress's name

explanation.surface: An actress swears while hosting a place.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash hides letters in the oath, but its last letter starts the run; H. Mirren is the actress Helen Mirren.
explanation.definitionFit: Kashmir is a disputed mountainous area in the north of the Indian subcontinent.

clue.text: Much drama from David

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the 1978 play by David Hare

explanation.surface: David, perhaps a dramatic friend, makes a big fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: David Hare is a leading British playwright; Plenty is one of his best-known plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenty means a lot, and it is also the title of a David Hare play about post-war Britain.

clue.text: A shit proposal

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a formal suggestion put to a meeting

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a rude verdict on someone's idea; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A motion is a bowel movement in medical language and also a proposal put to a vote in a debate.

clue.text: Live performing lifted little weight from the old PM

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifted letters go upwards, read from the bottom
taking something from a word removes it

parts.note: an actor who is performing is on stage
Tony Blair, former Prime Minister
lb is the abbreviation for a pound

explanation.surface: A live show where a small weight was lifted off a former Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' looks like taken away; it turns the pound abbreviation upside down so it matches the start of the PM's name, which then goes.
explanation.definitionFit: On air means being broadcast as it happens, which is what live means in radio and television.

clue.text: Liberal content of a whip's administrations

definitions.meaning: second meaning: strokes dealt out with a whip

explanation.surface: It sounds like the Liberal policy brought in by a party whip's governments.
explanation.walkthrough: Whip and Liberal suggest parliament, but the whip is a lash and liberal means plentiful.
explanation.definitionFit: Lashings is British for plenty, as in lashings of cream, and also a series of strokes with a whip.

clue.text: Brand created by him, Seb's moving in fashionable setting

indicators.note: one part is placed in the other, enclosed by it
a setting holds a jewel, so the outer word frames the moved letters

parts.note: in means fashionable

indicators.note: letters on the move change places

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A designer named Seb launches a fashion brand in a stylish setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brand' looks like a fashion label; it is a verse play of 1865.
explanation.definitionFit: Brand is a verse drama by the Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, so its creator is him.

clue.text: (& 10ac.) The new Boy George causing all this verbal nonsense?

definitions.text: The new Boy George causing all this
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the media chatter about the royal newborn
second meaning: the cooing, simplified speech used to infants

explanation.walkthrough: Boy George is a pop singer, but here it is the newborn Prince George, whose birth in 2013 set the press gushing.
explanation.definitionFit: Baby talk is the gooey nonsense language adults use with infants, and also all the gossip about a royal birth.

clue.text: He has the brass, etc. to deprive party leader of his left side — ace!

indicators.note: to deprive someone is to take something away from them
the left side of a name is its opening part, which is what goes

parts.note: Ed Miliband, then Labour leader
an ace is an expert, a master

explanation.surface: Someone with the cash is out to rob a party leader of his left-wing side, which would be ace.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Miliband led Labour; dropping his 'left' half MILI leaves BAND. 'The brass' looks like money but is the brass section.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandmaster conducts a band, so the brass and other sections are in his charge.

clue.text: Apology for crack showing outside an undergarment

indicators.note: one part is visible on the outside of another, wrapped round it

parts.note: to have a crack is to have a try
an is A
a vest is a sleeveless undershirt

explanation.surface: A plumber's crack peeping out over someone's underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' suggests a bottom showing; here it means an attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is a grotesque imitation, and 'an apology for' means a poor substitute for the real thing.

clue.text: Finish the last of the booze, producing tear (ironic)

definitions.text: Finish the last of the booze

parts.note: to tear along is to run
dry humour is ironic

explanation.surface: Draining the last drink brings someone to tears, ironically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' tempts as a teardrop; it is the verb meaning to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: To run dry is to be used up, as when a supply of drink is finished.
